an0697.user: Want a sharp read on this, not the obvious stuff. Haircare, mostly organic/SEO traffic. Last 30 days: 37,000 visits, 2,333 add-to-carts, 1,296 reached checkout, 401 purchases. CTR on listings around 1.7%. On paper acquisition looks fine to me — so where's the actual money leaking?
an0697.assistant:
Your acquisition isn't the problem — the top of this funnel is genuinely healthy. 2,333 add-to-carts on 37,000 visits is a 6.3% ATC rate, which for organic haircare traffic is good, not lucky. People want the product.

The leak is sitting at the very last step. Of the 1,296 who reached checkout, only 401 paid — that's a 31% checkout-to-purchase rate. A working checkout converts somewhere in the 50-70% band. You're losing roughly half the people who already pulled out their wallet and walked to the till. That's not a desire problem or a traffic-quality problem; that's friction in the final 20 seconds — a shipping cost that surprises them on the last screen, a forced account creation, or no UPI/COD where they expected it.

The one move: instrument the checkout before you touch anything upstream. Add event tracking on each checkout field, then watch a dozen session recordings of people who abandoned. Nine times out of ten you'll see them bounce the instant a ₹79 shipping line appears or a 'create password' box blocks them.

Don't spend another rupee on traffic — your ad and SEO money is already working. Caveat: 401 purchases is enough to trust the 31% figure, but session recordings will tell you the exact field they quit on faster than any aggregate number can.

an0699.user: Calm question, but it's been bugging me. D2C coffee, selling through Meesho Ads. AOV ₹750, gross margin 29%, CAC ₹410, ROAS sitting at 1.8, CTR 1.5%. I keep coming back to the same question — how do I get my CAC down?
an0699.assistant:
You're asking the wrong question, and I want to save you three months of chasing it. CAC isn't your disease — your margin is.

Run the contribution: ₹750 × 29% − ₹410 = ₹217.50 − ₹410 = −₹192 per order. You lose ₹192 every single time someone buys. No targeting tweak, no creative refresh, no audience exclusion fixes that, because the hole isn't in the ad account. Even if a brilliant optimisation cut CAC by ₹100, you'd still be at −₹92 — still underwater.

The mechanism is brutal and simple: a 29% gross margin only leaves you ₹217 to spend acquiring a customer, and you're spending ₹410. The ads are doing their job; the unit economics can't afford them.

The one lever is COGS, pricing, or AOV — not marketing. Get your margin from 29% toward the mid-40s, or lift AOV with bundles/larger packs so each order carries more rupees of contribution. At 45% margin, ₹750 × 45% = ₹337 — you're nearly breakeven on the same CAC.

Caveat: if there's real repeat-purchase behaviour you haven't shown me, LTV could partly rescue this. But on first-order economics, this is a margin problem wearing a marketing costume. Fix the margin first.

an0700.assistant:

That's the classic signature of saturation: you'd already captured your best, highest-intent audiences at the lower spend, and the extra ₹4.2L is buying colder, more expensive reach — people who were never going to convert as cheaply. Check where you still are: ₹1,100 × 65% = ₹715 contribution before CAC. At ₹886 CAC you're now −₹171 per order on the new spend, even though the original ₹554 cohort was +₹161. The marginal customer turned unprofitable; the average is just hiding it.

The lever isn't 'fix Meta' — it's create new demand before you add more budget. New audiences, genuinely new creative angles, or a second channel. More money into the same finite intent pool only buys you a worse CAC.

Pull spend back toward the ₹6L zone where the economics still worked, and use the saved budget to test the next audience. Caveat: confirm nothing else moved in week 4 — a creative going stale can mimic saturation — but the spend/CAC curve here is textbook ceiling.

an0701.user: Post-iOS mess, need someone to tell me what's wrong. Flipkart seller, running Amazon Ads. Spend ₹19.5L last 30 days. Platform dashboard says 4.3 ROAS. My Shopify last-click says 1.5 ROAS. Same campaigns, same period. The two numbers are nowhere near each other and I genuinely can't tell which one is the truth. What's wrong?
an0701.assistant:
Nothing's wrong with your campaigns — what's wrong is that you're refereeing two dashboards that will never agree, and treating one of them as gospel.

The platform's 4.3 is built on modelled conversions and a 7-day-click window — it generously claims credit for sales it merely touched. Shopify's last-click 1.5 does the opposite: it hands all the credit to whoever the customer clicked last, usually a branded search or direct visit, and starves your upper-funnel ads of any. Both are structurally biased. The real ROAS sits somewhere between 1.5 and 4.3, and no amount of staring will make either dashboard confess it.

Stop trying to crown a winner. Anchor on blended CAC instead: total spend across everything ÷ actual new customers Shopify recorded that month. On ₹19.5L, if you acquired, say, 1,300 new customers, that's a ₹1,500 blended CAC — one honest number you can manage to, immune to the attribution war. Set a target blended CAC tied to your contribution per order, and steer the whole budget to that.

Caveat: 'new customers' must mean first-time buyers, not all orders, or the number lies the other way. But blended CAC is the only metric here that isn't picking a side.

an0704.user: Quick one — candle brand on Google Search. Why is my CTR low at 1.4%? AOV is ₹2,700, margin 56%, CAC ₹738, ROAS 3.7. The 1.4% CTR is the thing bugging me, feels like it should be higher.

an0706.user: Eyewear brand, running Google Performance Max. Looking for the read that isn't obvious. Last 30 days: AOV ₹1,550, gross margin 62%, CAC ₹346, ROAS 4.5, CTR 1.8%. Repeat over 90 days is 9%. On the surface this looks like one of my best months — is it?

an0707.user: Skincare brand. Narrow question — why is my email CTR low? It's only 0.8%. Last 30 days, 880,000 impressions, 7,056 clicks, 73 orders, conversion rate about 1.03%, AOV ₹1,300. Running broad-match keywords. How do I lift that CTR?
an0707.assistant:
The CTR isn't your problem, so lifting it would just pour more of the wrong people onto your site. Let me show you where the real leak is.

You got 7,056 clicks and only 73 orders — that's a 1.03% conversion rate. The traffic is arriving; it just doesn't want to buy. That's the number to stare at, not the 0.8% CTR.

The cause is in your own description: broad-match keywords. Broad match throws you in front of a huge, loosely-related audience — people researching, comparing, idly curious about skincare in general, not someone ready to buy your serum. High impressions (880K), decent raw clicks, terrible intent. You're paying to attract browsers and then wondering why they don't check out.

The one lever: tighten the intent. Cut broad match to phrase/exact on your buying-intent terms, pile on negative keywords to block the research and freebie queries, and stop optimising the campaign toward clicks — optimise toward purchases. A smaller stream of high-intent traffic at 3-4% conversion beats this firehose at 1%.

Caveat: 73 orders is a thin month to draw a hard line, so make the match-type and negatives change, then judge it on the next ~100 orders, not next week.
